claims.text: A cluster-expansion-based machine-learning model augmented with targeted DFT and MD can accurately predict separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Above 300 K, lattice thermal transport dominates in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by at least 30% over conventional analytical models.
The intended samples span oxygen contents from nearly defect-free to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Refractory high-entropy alloys possess compositional complexity and local disorder that should be represented by the model.
Cluster expansion can represent chemical short-range order and configurational thermodynamics in a multicomponent alloy.
Force-constant fluctuations are relevant to phonon scattering in chemically disordered high-entropy alloys.
Adding oxygen-containing DFT and MD configurations will accurately capture oxygen-induced changes in local environments.
Local chemical short-range order and configurational ensembles modulate force-constant fluctuations.
Local chemical short-range order and configurational ensembles modulate electron-scattering pathways.
Representing short-range order, force-constant fluctuations, and electron-scattering pathways is critical for decoupling lattice and electronic heat transport.
Atomic-mass, force-constant-distribution, and short-range-order descriptors enable the machine-learning model to decouple lattice and electronic conduction.
Phonon spectra and anharmonic force constants derived from simulation can be used to predict lattice thermal conductivity.
DFT-derived band-structure descriptors can separately calculate the electronic thermal conductivity in the proposed model.
Earlier analytical estimates based on Debye approximations failed to capture oxygen-induced local disorder and produced conflated or less accurate transport descriptions.
The predictions apply to controlled-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr samples containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over 100–1200 K.
Applying the approach to other high-entropy-alloy systems would require reparameterization and additional training data.
TDTR combined with electrical-conductivity measurements and phonon spectroscopy can explicitly separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The hypothesis is falsified if separated conductivities differ from predictions by more than ±30% or if the predicted low- and high-temperature contribution behavior is absent.
